articles.title: Nepal floods: The remote Nepal-China border crossing at the heart of a Himalayan tragedy
articles.summary: More than 100 Indians are missing at a vital Nepal-China trade crossing after devastating Himalayan floods.
articles.body:
A dark wall appears from behind the buildings at Gyirong, on the Chinese side of the Nepal-Tibet border. At first, it looks almost like a black cloud. Then it gathers shape and speed: water, mud, boulders, ice and rock surging down the valley. The timestamp on the CCTV footage reads 10:59:53 local time.

What happened in the minutes that followed is still difficult to reconstruct. But fragments of video and satellite imagery from before and after the disaster have begun to reveal the scale of the destruction. Much of the border complex appears to have been swept away, with buildings that once crowded the valley floor simply gone.

Gyirong was one of the places devastated by the floods that tore through the region on 26 August.

Just across the frontier, at Rasuwagadhi in Nepal's Rasuwa district, the destruction was also extensive. The Friendship Bridge linking Nepal and China was swept away, along with Nepal's immigration and customs facilities. Timure, the small trading settlement clustered around the crossing, was devastated.

"This is a historic travel route between Kathmandu and Tibet. The area is geologically vulnerable, characterised by deep gorges and steep rivers that flow at high velocity, carry heavy sediment and can bring down huge boulders," says Ajay Dixit, a Kathmandu-based hydrologist.

The route remains an important gateway between Nepal and China. It is a place where pilgrims heading towards Mount Kailash cross paths with traders travelling between Nepal and China, truck drivers, customs officials, tourists and people who live along the border.

On the morning of the flood, more than 100 Indians may have been in or around the crossing. At least 275 Indians remain missing in Nepal, according to India's foreign ministry.

Nepal's Department of Immigration has been trying to reconstruct who passed through Rasuwagadhi in the final hours before the disaster.

Electronic records show that 89 Nepali and foreign nationals had cleared immigration to leave Nepal for Tibet, while four people had registered their entry into Nepal.

The immigration system recorded its final transaction at 8:35:03am local time (10:52am Tibet time), less than 10 minutes before the torrent appeared on the CCTV footage at Gyirong.

Four immigration employees, including the head of the Rasuwagadhi office, went missing in the floods. His body was later recovered far downstream. The female official who recorded the final transactions is still missing.

Among the foreign nationals recorded leaving Nepal that morning were 32 Indians, 12 Chinese nationals and nine Americans, as well as citizens of Britain, Canada, Australia and Italy.

Tika Ram Pokharel, a senior immigration assistant at Rasuwagadhi, was the only member of his office known to have survived. He had travelled to Kathmandu to sit an exam that day.

But he says the electronic records capture only part of what was happening at the border that morning.

The immigration office stood at Ghatte Khola Bazar, about 1.5km north of Timure. From there, it was another 2km to the Friendship Bridge marking the border with Tibet. Along that stretch were shops, hotels and parking areas where travellers and vehicles gathered before crossing.

The Nepalese immigration office opened at 08:00, Pokharel says. Once travellers had cleared immigration, they could continue towards the border or wait in the area before crossing.

When Pokharel called a colleague at 08:20 that morning, he was told the crossing was unusually busy. Around 300 to 400 people were waiting to leave Nepal for Tibet, he says, while others arriving from the Chinese side were also in the area.

"Those who completed the immigration formalities that morning, I don't think were able to complete their immigration process on the Chinese side," Pokharel told the BBC.

Pokharel says it took 15 to 20 minutes to walk from the Nepalese immigration office to the bridge after travellers had cleared immigration.

Travellers arriving late the previous afternoon sometimes had to wait until the border reopened the next morning, while those travelling in groups or by bus would often wait for everyone to clear immigration before moving on together.

That makes it difficult to know where those 89 people were when the flood struck.

At 8:37am - less than two minutes after the immigration system recorded its final transaction - seismic instruments detected movement in the mountains above the border, according to a timeline compiled by Nepal's Centre of Hydrology and Water Resources Research. Researchers later attributed the signal to the collapse of part of a glacier that triggered the flood.

China said the mudslide reached the border crossing from its origin in around seven minutes.

People at the crossing could have been making their way towards the bridge, waiting in Ghatte Khola or preparing to cross towards the Chinese facility. Exactly where each person was remains unclear.

And Ghatte Khola itself was far more than a waiting area. Pokharel says 50 to 60 houses stood there, alongside hotels, local businesses and four hydropower offices.

It was also the final stop for buses from Kathmandu, and a base for drivers, helpers, tourist guides and cargo workers waiting for customs clearance. Travellers heading into Tibet often queued there from the previous day.

"My 40-50 close friends are missing," Pokharel said.

Pokharel believes the toll there could be far higher than official figures suggest, estimating that "2,000 to 2,500 people" may have been caught in the flood. The figure is his estimate and has not been independently verified.

The immigration office itself stood about 100 metres above the river, Pokharel says. But during the flood, the water appeared to surge even higher. He initially hoped his missing colleagues might have escaped to grazing land several kilometres away.

For some of the Indian pilgrims at the border, the morning had begun almost casually. They made video calls and reels for relatives back home, showing them the mountains as they waited for the Chinese immigration office to open.

Sudipto Bhattacharya was receiving messages from his wife, Subhrasree Chakraborty, who was travelling with a group of more than 60 people. At 07:57 Nepal time, she sent him a photograph of the departure stamp in her passport: Nepalese immigration was done.

Six minutes later, at 08:03, she sent another message: "We are waiting to enter China." Then the messages stopped.

Among those at the Chinese immigration facility was a group of 77 pilgrims associated with the Isha Foundation, returning from Mount Kailash. They, along with three staff members, were unaccounted for after the flood swept through the area.

When a 21-member Chinese rescue team reached Gyirong on 28 August, one rescuer told Chinese state media: "As far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins."

The crossing had only recently recovered from another major flood. In July 2025, flooding shut Rasuwagadhi for nearly six months. It reopened on 1 January after China built a temporary bridge.

Traffic had since returned. Chinese border authorities say more than 100,000 people had passed through Gyirong by June, while Nepali immigration records show 53,742 arrivals and departures at Rasuwagadhi in the year to mid-July. The two figures are based on different reporting periods and counting systems, making a direct comparison difficult.

Indians were the largest group recorded at the Nepali immigration point, followed by Nepalis and Chinese.

Gyirong had also become one of the main arteries linking Nepal and China.

Posh Raj Pandey, chairman emeritus of the Kathmandu-based South Asia Watch on Trade, Economics and Environment, says Rasuwagadhi is one of Nepal's two main trading points with China, alongside Tatopani, and accounts for about a third of Nepal's $2.95bn trade with its northern neighbour.

Around 60 to 70 trucks passed through the gorge each day, carrying electronics, machinery, vehicles, fruit, clothing and other goods towards Kathmandu. Pandey says the route also handled about 80% of Nepal's electric-vehicle imports from China.

Its closure has left Nepal increasingly dependent on Tatopani - which Chinese authorities have also temporarily closed because of landslide risks on the Nepali side, the Kathmandu Post reports.

The crossing also lies along the proposed route of the railway connecting the region to Kathmandu, part of plans by Nepal and China to develop a trans-Himalayan rail network.

"Nepal should develop an alternative China trade route and reconsider its wider development strategy, including its heavy concentration of hydropower projects along the same river system," Pandey says.

"We have put all eggs here. We need to develop an alternative border port."

Across the border, Pokharel was left thinking about conversations he had with the colleagues who were now missing.

The previous year's flood had made staff at the Rasuwagadhi immigration office acutely aware of the danger. At night, he says, they sometimes "felt vibrations" and went outside to check the river. They had even discussed among themselves about escaping uphill if another flood struck.

"But my friends could not get that chance," he said.

articles.title: Russian attack hits rail workers in new deadly strikes on Kyiv
articles.summary: Ukrainian officials say 20 people, including two children, were injured in the capital and the wider region.
articles.body:
At least 12 people have been killed and 20 injured, including two children, in overnight Russian missile and drone strikes on Ukraine's capital Kyiv and the wider region, officials say.

Six of the casualties were railway workers of the state Ukrzaliznytsia company after a depot was hit in Kyiv.

Russia said its "massive strike using high-precision weapons" targeted Ukraine's military and energy facilities, and added that one person was also killed in Ukrainian strikes on Russia's western Belgorod region.

This comes a day after Russian President Vladimir Putin was urged by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a close ally, to end the war.

"Every day spent in war pushes humanity back, and every step taken towards peace fills humanity with new hope and enthusiasm," Modi said at a security summit in Kyrgyzstan.

Modi, whose country's economy depends heavily on discounted oil from Moscow, has made several similar pleas to Putin since he launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Overnight in Kyiv, eight people were killed and fires were reported in three city districts.

Another four people were killed in the nearby town of Boryspil where a residential building was hit.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Tuesday morning that nearly 350 rescue workers had been working through the night in Kyiv and the surrounding region after the latest strikes.

In a post on social media, he said Russia had fired a "significant number of jet drones and ballistic missiles".

The strikes mark the sixth day of sustained Russian drone and missile attacks on Kyiv, in what appears to be a strategy aimed at exhausting Ukrainian air defences and undermining civilian morale.

Russia's military warned over the weekend that its forces were preparing to carry out "massive" strikes on Ukrainian energy facilities.

Eight other Ukrainian regions were attacked, Zelensky said, adding that an Indian national was among the casualties.

Ukraine's Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivsky later said the Indian man - who turned 26 on Tuesday - was killed in Boryspil.

The overnight attacks come after 38 people were killed in Russian strikes on a weapons depot in the Kyiv region on Friday, causing shells, mines and drones to detonate.

Separately, a drone attack hit a major Russian Baltic Sea port in Ust-Luga, triggering a fire, Leningrad regional Governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said.

Ukraine says targets like Ust-Luga - which handles millions of tons of petroleum products each year - are legitimate as they help finance Moscow's war effort.

articles.title: Ex-gang leader Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis found guilty of murdering Tupac Shakur
articles.summary: Jury finds Duane “Keffe D” Davis, 63, guilty of murdering the chart-topping artist in the 1996 shooting.
articles.body:
A former gang leader accused of orchestrating the killing of hip-hop star Tupac Shakur in the United States in 1996 ⁠has been convicted of murder for his role in the long-unsolved crime.

A jury in Clark County, Nevada, deliberated for nearly three hours on Monday before finding Duane “Keffe D” Davis, 63, guilty of a single count of first-degree ⁠murder with a deadly weapon, capping an 11-day trial in a courtroom in the city of Las Vegas.

Davis will face a maximum sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole at his sentencing on October 13. He told the judge “he plans to appeal this matter”.

Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips street gang in Los Angeles, was accused of ordering the drive-by shooting that killed Shakur on September 7, 1996. Prosecutors said he was enraged because members of Shakur’s entourage had beaten his nephew at a Las Vegas casino hours earlier.

“Duane Davis, in the culture of gangs, could not let that stand,” prosecutor Binu Palal said during closing arguments. “So what did he do? He acquired a firearm, got his group together and went hunting for Mr Shakur.”

Shakur, who was in Las Vegas for a Mike Tyson heavyweight fight, was shot about two hours after the casino confrontation by a gunman in a white Cadillac that pulled up at a red light alongside the BMW in which the rapper was riding in the front passenger seat.

According to prosecutors, Davis handed the gun to someone sitting in the back seat of the Cadillac and ordered that person to shoot Shakur, who died six days later.

Davis is the only person who was in the Cadillac that evening who is still alive.

The driver of the BMW, Death Row Records cofounder Marion “Suge” Knight, was wounded.

The killing of Shakur, also known as 2Pac, has been one of the US’s most notorious cold cases, prompting endless debate among music fans over who did it and why.

The investigation into Shakur’s murder sputtered for decades because of a lack of evidence, but the case was revived when Davis’s memoirs were published in 2019. Davis has repeatedly boasted over the years of involvement in Shakur’s murder, in interviews with law enforcement and media and ultimately in his autobiography, Compton Street Legend.

He has since backtracked and pleaded not guilty to the murder charge.

Palal, the prosecutor, played clips from Davis’s various alleged confessions as part of his closing arguments.

Michael Sanft, Davis’s defence attorney, characterised his client’s confessions as fiction and lies partly designed to promote his book.

“You’re reading a book that is fiction and not fact,” Sanft told the jury. “But the state wants you to believe that this is somehow a confession, that he was there and present at the time of the shooting.”

Sanft said there was no evidence implicating Davis in Shakur’s murder other than his own statements.

In the run-up to the trial, Davis’s lawyers tried in vain to keep the book from being introduced as evidence, along with remarks he made in an interview with police in 2008.

Shakur, who was 25 when he was killed, was a key figure in a hip-hop rivalry pitting US East Coast rappers against West Coast artists.

Known for hits including “California Love” and “All Eyez on Me”, Shakur – the son of a Black Panther – was raised in Harlem and Baltimore, but became the epitome of California hip-hop when he signed with Los Angeles-based Death Row Records.

articles.title: How prices in Tunisia have skyrocketed since the Arab Spring
articles.summary: Al Jazeera tracked the cost of common food items and compared them with pre-revolution prices in 2010.
articles.body:
In Tunisia, the cost-of-living crisis has outlasted the government it once toppled.

On December 17, 2010, street vendor Mohamed Bouazizi set himself on fire in Sidi Bouzid following years of police harassment, setting off protests driven by unemployment, corruption, rising living costs and police brutality.

The movement, which became known as the Arab Spring, ultimately toppled longtime President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali and four other leaders around the Arab world.

Nearly 16 years later, however, Tunisians are still facing a cost-of-living crisis that some say is worse than ever.

To show how much everyday prices have changed, Al Jazeera tracked the cost of common food items and compared them with their 2010 prices.

Dinar has lost half its value against the dollar

In December 2010, one United States dollar bought 1.47 Tunisian dinars. Today it buys 2.93, meaning each dinar is only worth half (49 percent) the dollar value it was worth 15 years ago.

Tunisia buys much of its food abroad and pays for it in dollars and euros. A weaker dinar means each of those purchases costs more, and shoppers see it at the till.

Prices at the supermarket tell the story.

In 2010, eight Tunisian dinars bought 4kg (8.8lb) of tomatoes, half a kg (1.1lb) of chicken and a litre (34oz) of cooking oil. Today the same eight dinars buys less than half of that. The price of tomatoes has risen 113 percent; chicken, 118 percent; and cooking oil, 129 percent.

Prices of vegetables have climbed higher still. Carrots now cost 428 percent more (that is more than five times) than they did in 2010, potatoes 268 percent. Beef, already the most expensive item on the list, has risen 290 percent (nearly four times) to 52.5 dinars a kg – or about $18.

Rice, still tightly price-controlled, is the outlier at 10 percent higher.

Abdessattar*, 55, from El Jem, says that with the exception of subsidised goods, the increases are hard to miss. “You feel that 20, 30 or 40 dinars don’t buy much any more,” he tells Al Jazeera. Butter, cheese, cleaning products and school snacks have all risen in price since last year.

The graphic below sets average 2010 prices from the Tunisian monthly statistics bulletin against those recorded this week.

Tunisia has subsidised basic food items since 1970, when it established the General Compensation Fund (Caisse Generale de Compensation). The state holds prices for certain staples below market rate and pays producers and importers the difference.

Items have been removed from the list over the decades, however. In late 2022, the government agreed to gradually phase out universal food subsidies in favour of targeted cash transfers to secure an IMF loan, but President Kais Saied halted the implementation of these terms in 2023.

The result is a two-tier basket: Subsidised goods have kept their fixed prices, while unsubsidised food prices have surged.

‘The results were really, really disappointing’

Hamed el-Matri is an engineer and political activist who now lives in Qatar. He was in Tunisia during the 2010 uprising and says he was on its front lines.

El-Matri recalls how the uprising was driven by socioeconomic demands, including jobs, freedom and dignity.

“The expectations at the time were very high. But, when I see the situation today, or even across the last 15 years, the results were really, really disappointing,” he tells Al Jazeera.

El-Matri says the 15 years cannot be treated as one period. He describes 2011 to 2021 as “a stumbling democratic transition” and what followed as “a kind of populist totalitarian rule, with a very aggressive rhetoric but quite unclear policy”.

El-Matri says that over the past five years, economic systems in Tunisia have more than weakened, if not collapsed. He explains that investment has almost stopped, and the economy is not far from stagnation.

‘Public transport is no longer reliable’

Yassine*, 44, a father in Tunis, says preparing his children for the new school year has become a source of anxiety. Subsidised notebooks and other cheap school supplies have disappeared from shops, he says, and families are buying second-hand books and materials from one another instead.

Transport is another worry. “Public transport is no longer reliable, so we’re forced to use private transport. It has become a major worry for every Tunisian,” he says.

He points to cooking oil, which once cost one dinar per litre but is now sold only in a version costing five dinars a litre.

The strain shows at every occasion. During the recent Eid holidays, Yassine says, most people he knew could not celebrate properly, and many bought second-hand clothes.

Hanen*, 45, a factory worker in Tunis, told Al Jazeera that prices have risen so fast that “people can no longer meet basic needs”. Red meat, which once sold for 20 dinars per kg, now costs 60 or more, she says, and the price of medicine climbs daily. Staples including canned tomatoes, sugar and cooking oil have all gone up sharply, along with fruit and vegetables. “The price hikes are extreme. It’s abnormal,” she says.

*Some names have been changed for anonymity.

articles.title: Zambia's President Hakainde Hichilema sworn in for second term while opponent detained
articles.summary: Hakainde Hichilema swept to victory, but his main rival is now in custody charged with treason.
articles.body:
Zambia's President Hakainde Hichilema has been sworn in for a second five-year term following a disputed election and the arrest of his main opponent on treason charges.

Hichilema - credited with stabilising the economy - swept to victory on 13 August with 60% of the vote, according to official results. Runner-up Brian Mundubile, who received 38%, alleged that the outcome had been tampered with.

He was unable to mount a legal challenge to the result as the courts were sealed off last week on the final day a case could be filed.

Election observers said that while polling day was largely peaceful, some have raised questions about the vote tallying process.

European Union observers said staff in many tallying centres did not record results on tally sheets as soon as they were announced and cited weak verification between digital entries and paper records.

It added that returning officers frequently paused proceedings while awaiting instructions from headquarters.

The day after the poll, security forces raided a property in the capital, Lusaka, linked to Mundubile, killing a former cabinet minister and arresting a number of opposition politicians.

The authorities accused the opposition of planning an armed insurrection, which they denied.

Mundubile and his running mate, Makebi Zulu, had gone into hiding. They were detained by police last week and charged at the weekend.

When Hichilema, 64, came into office in 2021 after a landslide victory, Zambia had recently defaulted on its international debt and had an annual inflation rate of more than 24%.

"We inherited a broken-down country… the economy was declining," Hichilema told the BBC in Lusaka before the election.

The former businessman negotiated a restructuring of the debt and rebuilt relations with foreign creditors. Inflation has also come down, but prices are still rising and many continue to struggle with the cost of living.

Hichilema now wants to build on the foundations he said he laid over the past five years.

He was sworn into office on Tuesday amid jubilant scenes, as thousands of supporters gathered to celebrate the inauguration.

Presidents from Kenya, Botswana, Zimbabwe, Namibia and Tanzania are among several African leaders attending the inauguration ceremony at the National Heroes Stadium in the capital.

Hichilema was sworn in alongside his running mate, Mutale Nalumango.

articles.title: Duolingo D-Day: Iranians question latest US sanctions targeting education
articles.summary: Many Iranians inside the country feel they are being unjustly erased from the international community.
articles.body:
Tehran, Iran – When the United States threatened an “economic D-Day” for Iran, announcing a series of new sanctions against Tehran, President Donald Trump’s administration said it was seeking to cripple its adversary economically.

To many Iranians, though, the latest measures also appear targeted at them, rather than the Iranian government and its leadership.

Like previous waves of sanctions imposed by the US and its allies on Iran, the latest measures again disproportionately impact the country’s civilian population. And one sector in particular appears poised to take a major hit: education.

Previous sanctions have contributed to making Iranians poorer by triggering a currency collapse, leading to surging food and medicine prices. They have financially isolated Iranians through blocked bank transfers and digital exclusion through restricted software, cloud services and platforms. The US travel ban , which counts Iran among its primary targets, has dashed countless dreams.

But the latest steps go one step further, and come at a time when the Iranian government has also ramped up domestic pressure .

New sanctions on assets, education and sport

As part of “Operation Economic Outcast”, the Trump administration last week expanded secondary sanctions in five more key economic sectors impacting civilian life — aviation, digital assets, gold, shipping and technology.

Those sectors were added to a comprehensive list that includes financial sectors, construction and manufacturing, among others. Any person anywhere in the world operating in, or engaging in any significant transaction with, or providing any assistance to anyone operating in those sectors may be designated as a blocked party under US secondary sanctions.

That could bring about asset freezes and an effective quarantine from US-linked and much of global commerce. That is why, despite some humanitarian-linked protections, the years-long “maximum pressure” campaign of the US against Iran has had wide-ranging impacts on civilian life, including availability of some medicine and medical equipment .

Last week, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) of the US Treasury also indefinitely suspended education-related general licences that permitted limited cooperation with Iran by American universities or people, including but not limited to academic exchange programmes and certain nonprofit education services.

The US also indefinitely suspended another general licence that permitted services in support of professional and amateur sports activities and exchanges involving Iran.

Another suspension targets services related to conferences in the US or third parties, while OFAC also suspended its permissions for certain non-commercial, personal remittances to or from people in Iran.

A very short wind-down period has been set for existing activities in all those areas until September 8, after which activities will require specific OFAC authorisation.

Washington has further emphasised that both US and non-US people anywhere risk being sanctioned if they engage with Iran or its Persian Gulf Strait Authority and other organisations in connection with obtaining guarantees of safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz.

As part of its latest economic measures, the US has contacted Iran’s neighbours to limit trade, targeted the operations of Egypt’s second-biggest bank in the United Arab Emirates and is considering action against another bank .

The stated goal of the operation is to sever every economic lifeline sustaining Iran’s government and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) in order to coerce them into shifting their behaviour.

But the suspension of General License G, which permitted education-related activities, is already quietly impacting thousands of young Iranians who have no links to the government.

Educational Testing Service (ETS), the nonprofit organisation which holds TOEFL and GRE language exams required to get into thousands of universities worldwide, this week paused administration of the tests in Iran and cancelled previously booked test appointments.

“This step reflects our full compliance with US sanctions law,” an ETS spokesperson told Al Jazeera in an emailed statement, adding that Iranian nationals can test outside of Iran.

“We are actively working to understand the scope and duration of this change and pursue any available paths to resume service, allowing learners to continue their educational journey uninterrupted.”

Duolingo, the American educational technology company that offers learning apps and language certifications, decided to go one step further than ETS by banning English language tests for all users holding only an Iranian ID – meaning that Iranian passport holders outside the country would also be rejected.

“Following an August 24 action by the US Treasury Department, Duolingo is required to stop offering the Duolingo English Test to people testing in Iran or using Iranian government-issued identification beginning September 1. This includes people outside Iran who need to use Iranian government-issued ID,” the company said in an emailed statement to Al Jazeera.

“We recognise that changes to test availability can be disappointing for affected test takers. We have contacted those with active credits directly about completing their tests or receiving refunds.”

Duolingo said in its statement that it does not know “whether or when the regulations may change”, and would “reassess the test’s availability” if circumstances changed.

Over recent days, many Iranians who were planning to obtain language certificates – whether to leave Iran, participate in international scholarships and research or seek better employment – were taken by surprise by the latest impact of sanctions.

In a Telegram group for people wishing to take the TOEFL test, which has 25,000 members, frustrated, panicked and dejected users have been reflecting on the news this week and speculating about what more could be in store over the coming years as the war with the US drags on after more than six months.

Some only know that they do not want that future to be inside tumultuous Iran.

“I couldn’t stop crying for two days, but so what? I won’t let it stop my plans for going to an English-language country or Germany as a backup. They [my plans] will be delayed at best,” said Faezeh, who added that she is now forced to calculate the additional costs of going to Turkiye, Armenia or other regional countries to take the test, even as the Iranian economy falters .

Some are now creating petitions and gathering signatures in long-shot attempts at overturning the restrictions, while others are calling on millions of diaspora Iranians to raise awareness or downvoting Duolingo on app stores.

Regardless of whether people can afford to or be able to overcome the mounting obstacles, many say they are being discriminated against based on their nationality, without any perceivable harm coming to the leaders and institutions of the government.

“Truly, who are these types of sanctions hurting? It feels like they are taking Iranians out of the list of accepted human species,” Danial, a young Tehran-based man considering moving away from Iran in search of a more stable life, told Al Jazeera.

He pointed out that the IELTS language test was also suspended for Iranians inside the country in January, blocking another major pathway. He said students looking to pursue academic degrees outside Iran have been watching other developments with concern, including several universities in Australia, Norway and the United Kingdom pausing PhD applications, sponsorships or enrollment for Iranians in recent months.

Many Iranians reacting to the news online this week said the latest impact of the sanctions was particularly jarring since, in January, when thousands were killed during nationwide antigovernment protests in Iran, the US president said: “help is on its way.”

The Trump administration has also tried to make a distinction between the majority of Iranian people and the government, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying in February he knows of “no other country where there’s a bigger difference between the people who lead the country and the people who live there”.

“Iran is officially a Failed Nation. IT IS DEAD!” Trump wrote in a post online on Monday.

articles.title: Death toll from devastating floods in Nepal surpasses 1,000
articles.summary: Rescue efforts continue to focus on hydropower sites, where hundreds of workers are believed to be trapped.
articles.body:
The death toll from catastrophic flooding in Nepal and China has reached 1,019, and more than 4,400 people remain missing as rescue crews work to reach communities cut off by the disaster.

In an update on Tuesday, Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) increased the number of deaths from 987 to 1,003, with 3,916 people missing , including 583 foreigners.

Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 people still missing, including 261 foreigners, in their most recent update on Sunday.

The disaster hit on August 26 , beginning with a chain of events high in the Himalayas, when a glacial collapse sent large amounts of rock, ice, and meltwater into valleys below, triggering powerful floods downstream.

Scientists studying satellite imagery said the collapse appears to have involved the failure of bedrock beneath a glacier.

Hundreds of workers are feared to be trapped in tunnels at several devastated hydropower stations in Nepal that have become the focus of rescue efforts .

Prime Minister Balendra Shah said 279 workers had been rescued from hydropower projects so far, where authorities had initially estimated that more than 900 people were missing.

More than 11,000 people have been rescued across the affected region, and power and communication lines have been restored in some areas, he added.

“Thousands of citizens have lost their homes, families, loved ones, and property,” Shah said on social media.

“The government understands the immense pain they are enduring. The path ahead is to support them through this suffering and help them return to normal life through rehabilitation.”

Rescue teams had managed to restore road networks to Nuwakot, one of the worst-affected districts, facilitating rescue operations and the distribution of relief material, Shah said.

Police official Bipin Regmi said a search team recovered 24 bodies from a house in Betrabati village in Nuwakot district.

“We are reaching new areas and recovering bodies,” Regmi told the Reuters news agency.

Aid worth more than $42m has poured into the country after the disaster, Shah said, and the government expects the contributions to increase.

Neighbours India and China are helping with rescue efforts, including building Bailey bridges to reach remote affected areas.

Pictures and videos shared by rescue teams showed earth-moving equipment digging and shovelling mud and rocks under lights in the dark of the night as workers watched.

Soldiers used torchlight in a big pit they had created to look for space to get into one tunnel.

There has been a boom in hydropower projects in Nepal since the turn of the century, as the mountainous country sought to take advantage of its Himalayan water resources to address chronic domestic power shortages and exploit prospects for selling electricity to its southern neighbour, India.

Hydropower projects in Nepal’s mountains need tunnels to carry water through the steep terrain, allowing developers to exploit the sharp elevation drop between Himalayan rivers and powerhouses to generate electricity.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy jury set to deliberate for another day
articles.summary: Jurors in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial are set to enter their fourth day of deliberations Tuesday over whether to hold her criminally responsible for killing her three young children at her Massachusetts home in 2023.
articles.body: PLYMOUTH, Mass. — Jurors in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial are set to enter their fourth day of deliberations Tuesday over whether to hold her criminally responsible for killing her three young children at her Massachusetts home in 2023. The jury began deliberating in secret last Thursday. It has been quiet since then, with no communications to the judge suggesting how things might be going. Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse, does not deny strangling her children but says postpartum psychosis led to her actions. Prosecutors argue she knew what she was doing. Clancy, 36, has pleaded not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility. The jury could convict her of murder or manslaughter, or acquit her if they believe her deteriorating mental health was to blame. A conviction could lead to a life prison sentence. If she is acquitted, a judge could still order her confined to a mental health facility if an evaluation determines she is a danger to the public. Clancy’s lawyer argued at the trial that she loved her children, but killed them because she lost her grip on reality — and on herself — due to postpartum psychosis, a rare mental illness that can follow childbirth. In the months before the killings, Clancy sought treatment for her worsening mental health, including a stay in a psychiatric hospital. Prosecutors said Clancy strangled the children because she was depressed and tired of living, and made a conscious choice to kill them before attempting suicide.

articles.title: Leaders of China, Russia and India meet to counter U.S. influence
articles.summary: The leaders of China, Russia and India gathered with other heads of state in Kyrgyzstan for the summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, a group billed as a counterweight to U.S. global influence.
articles.body: The leaders of China, Russia and India gathered with other heads of state in Kyrgyzstan on Monday for the summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, a group billed as a counterweight to U.S. global influence. Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi are attending the events in Bishkek, the capital of the Central Asian nation. Putin met separately with Xi and Modi in two of the many bilateral sessions on the sidelines of the summit. Putin affirmed to Xi Moscow’s readiness to make the visa-free regime with China permanent, and he said Russia’s relationship with India is strengthening. Talks between Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian are expected Tuesday, the day of the official SCO sessions. Russia, now 4½ years into its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and Iran, six months into a war with the United States and Israel, see the summit as an important platform to strengthen their relations with non-Western partners. Modi told Putin through a translator that India supports efforts to end the war in Ukraine, and that “we need to move from endless war to the end of war, to the end of hostilities,” adding that “this is very important for all of humanity.” The SCO was founded in 2001 by China, Russia and four Central Asian states as a security forum. Over the past quarter-century, it has grown in size and influence, although its goals and programs remain vague and its brand recognition low. It now includes 10 nations: Russia, China, India, Iran, Pakistan, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. Many other countries have the status of “dialogue partners.” Along with Russia, China has presented the SCO as an alternative to Western-aligned organizations like the G7, and in recent years has wanted to expand the scope and influence of the organization, pledging development and financial assistance. China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said last week that the organization has successfully “explored a new path for regional cooperation.” Beijing has consistently promoted the idea of an alternative world order with Russia’s support. Summit attendees have significant disagreements For many SCO members, the summit will be an opportunity to show that they maintain strong ties on the global stage despite souring relations with the West. The organization is not a unified political or military bloc, however, and analysts note that its members have significant disagreements and their own distinct interests. For countries such as India, however, experts say the summit is likely to be more about optics and strategic signaling than substantive outcomes. The forum is heavily influenced by China and includes Pakistan as a member — both of which are rivals of India. Dinakar Peri, a fellow in security studies at Carnegie India, said the SCO gives India a seat at the table in a region increasingly shaped by competition among the larger powers, allowing it to protect its interests, track shifting geopolitical currents and project itself as a reliable stakeholder. “While it may not entirely shape the agenda, it gives New Delhi a first-hand view of the region and allows it to hedge its position with others,” Peri said. Turkey, which holds partner status within the SCO, also seeks to use the platform to strengthen its position in the region. It views SCO membership as part of a balanced foreign policy that seeks to maintain its traditional ties with the West as a part of NATO, while strengthening its influence in Eurasia. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who brought his country into the SCO as a “dialogue partner” in 2012, has repeatedly stated that he wants Turkey to become a permanent member. While Turkey has close trade ties with the European Union under a 1995 trade deal, its EU membership bid has stalled for more than 25 years. Security restrictions imposed in Bishkek Major shopping malls, markets and other sites in the capital were closed for the duration of the summit as part of security measures, and commercial flights to and from Manas Airport were restricted. “Traffic in central Bishkek will be regularly restricted,” said Askat Alagozov, a spokesman for Kyrgyz President Sadyr Zhaparov, urging residents to leave the city. The start of the school year was postponed until Sept. 15, and authorities declared Tuesday a non-working day for public sector and civil servants in Bishkek.

articles.title: In 2024, Melinda French Gates walked away from the foundation that carried her name, took $12.5 billion with her, and is now spending those billions on ...
articles.summary: Tech News News: Melinda French Gates resigned from the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation in May 2024, three years after her divorce, taking $12.5 billion with her to .
articles.body: Melinda French Gates resigned from the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation in May 2024, three years after her divorce, taking $12.5 billion with her to direct independently. Rather than spreading that money across a broad portfolio of causes, Melinda Gates decided to single at one and narrow the target to women and girls and specifically the parts of that problem that have historically gone chronically underfunded, according to a report by Startup Fortune. French Gates has consistently directed her money towards the underfunded areas such as menopause research, childcare infrastructure, domestic workers and representation of women in finance and media. Gates approach avoid popular causes which already attract a lot of funding making sure that each dollar makes maximum impact.Melinda Gates wants to tackle time povertyPhilanthropist Melinda French Gates frequently returns to on major statistic which is the International Labour Organisation (ILO). The ILO has estimated that women and girls collectively perform 12.5 billion hours of unpaid work every day which includes cooking, cleaning, childcare and care of elderly people. Before the pandemic, women were already taking care of roughly three-quarters of unpaid household labor, and that share has since increased rather than declined.She has a specific term for the consequence of that imbalance: time poverty, a concept she first raised publicly in the Gates Foundation's 2016 annual letter, well before it became a widely discussed topic. Her argument isn't framed primarily as a moral one, though it carries that dimension too — it's structural. Unpaid care work effectively subsidizes the global economy while simultaneously excluding hundreds of millions of people from paid work, education, and positions where real decisions get made. Without that "second shift" being addressed, building a career, finishing an education, or taking on real responsibility becomes far harder, which is why her funding has consistently gravitated toward childcare systems and paid family leave rather than more visible, easily celebrated causes.Where did Melinda Gates actually donated her moneyHer headline pledge was $1 billion in 2024, allocated as follows:* US organizations such as the National Women’s Law Center and Center for Reproductive Rights received $200 million.* Global leaders including Jacinda Ardern and Shabana Basij-Rasikh were each given $20 million to direct independently.* Open call funding invited applications worldwide for women’s health projects, with $250 million set aside.In June 2026, she added $215 million for reproductive and midlife health, including menopause research, followed by another $10 million at a benefit concert with Olivia Rodrigo.Why she targets underfunded causes over popular onesThe recurring pattern in French Gates's giving is a consistent preference for what's underfunded over what's popular — menopause research, domestic workers, childcare infrastructure, and women's political representation in finance and media. These aren't causes that generate easy applause at a gala, which is precisely why funding gaps exist around them in the first place, and precisely why money directed there tends to produce outsized impact relative to money aimed at more crowded, already well-funded causes.The second consistent element of her approach is funding at a scale large enough to change what recipients are able to attempt, rather than distributing smaller amounts thinly enough to keep many organizations modestly funded. A $20 million fund given to a single leader to deploy at their own discretion functions very differently than twenty separate $1 million grants carrying individual reporting requirements — one approach enables sustained activity, while the other creates the conditions for a genuinely ambitious attempt at change.The specific thesis behind French Gates donating moneyFrench Gates's giving is organized around a specific thesis: that women's economic power, health, and political representation are really the same underlying problem viewed from three different angles, and that progress on any one of them remains fragile without progress on the other two as well. Health without economic power leaves people dependent on others. Economic power without political representation means outside parties continue writing the rules. And representation without health or financial security simply isn't accessible to most of the population in the first place.That framework is why her funding spans all three areas simultaneously, channeled through Pivotal, the philanthropic organization she founded in 2015 — years before her divorce gave her independent control over her share of the Gates fortune. That timing matters: her current giving strategy isn't a reaction to a personal life event, but the execution of a decade-old conviction that only recently gained control of its own capital.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: In 1989, businessman Adrian Gardiner bought a roughly 3,000-acre South African farm as a family retreat; it grew into a 61,800-acre reserve supporting more than 5,000 animals
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Adrian Gardiner bought a single farm in South Africa’s Eastern Cape in 1989 as a weekend retreat for his family. The property covered about 1,200 hect.
articles.body: Adrian Gardiner bought a single farm in South Africa’s Eastern Cape in 1989 as a weekend retreat for his family. The property covered about 1,200 hectares, but Gardiner soon began buying neighbouring farms and looking at what the land had been like before years of agriculture, hunting and drought caused a reduction in its wildlife.That project became Shamwari Game Reserve, which today covers about 25,000 hectares, or roughly 61,800 acres, in the Eastern Cape. The reserve is now home to more than 5,000 head of game, according to conservation and tourism records.A family farm became a larger planThe official history of Founders Lodge says that Gardiner bought the Eastern Cape farm as a family weekend retreat in 1989, and three years later, he founded Shamwari Game Reserve. In a 2013 interview with Rhino Africa, he said he kept buying farms until he had accumulated about 10,000 hectares and realised he needed to find a way to use the land. The property had been heavily farmed and overgrazed, which left Gardiner with a landscape that required more than simply putting animals back onto it.Upon researching the region’s earlier wildlife, it was found that species such as lions and other large animals had once occupied the area. Gardiner decided to try to rebuild that ecosystem rather than continue using the land as conventional farmland.Rebuilding an ecosystemGardiner worked with conservationists, including Ian Player, on the effort to recreate parts of the Eastern Cape ecosystem, and this involved more than introducing large mammals. Rhino Africa’s account describes the process as rebuilding an entire ecological system, which began with plant and insect life and eventually extended to larger animals. Gardiner recalled that wild dogs introduced to the property killed large numbers of prey animals because they could use the reserve’s fences to their advantage during hunts, and managing the returning wildlife became part of the broader conservation work.The reserve finally reached a point where it could support large predators, and in October 2000, the first lions were reintroduced to Shamwari as part of a systematic wildlife program. The effort was also tied to tourism, since Gardiner wanted the reserve to generate enough income to sustain conservation, rather than depend entirely on outside funding. The model combined wildlife restoration with safari lodges and employment for people from surrounding communities.From farmland to 25,000 hectaresShamwari opened to its first guests in October 1992, when the reserve consisted of a single lodge and game drives across about 3,500 hectares of restored farmland. The property continued to expand as more surrounding farms were purchased and rehabilitated. Shamwari’s own account says the reserve eventually grew to its current 25,000 hectares, which is equivalent to about 61,800 acres, more than 20 times the size of the original 1,200-hectare farm Gardiner bought in 1989.Earlier conservation records put the wildlife number at more than 5,000 head of game, which included animals that were bred on the reserve and species brought back through reintroduction programs. The project eventually became associated with the return of the Big Five (lion, leopard, elephant, rhino and buffalo) to an area where intensive farming had greatly reduced wildlife.The project expanded well beyond ShamwariGardiner later became involved in other conservation and tourism projects and founded the Mantis Collection in 2000, building a group of hotels, lodges and game reserves around conservation-led tourism. He provided space to the Born Free Foundation for lions and leopards rescued from captivity, which gave the animals large enclosures in the Eastern Cape rather than returning them to conventional captive facilities.He sold Shamwari in 2008 but retained a portion of the original family property, and that land became the Founders Reserve, next to Shamwari, while the Gardiner family home was eventually converted into Founders Lodge. The lodge opened to guests in 2016 after 21 years as the family’s private home. Shamwari now operates as a private game reserve in the Eastern Cape, with its 25,000-hectare footprint incorporating restored former farmland and wildlife habitat.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Britons face ‘risk premium’ for energy as US-Israel war on Iran intensifies
articles.summary: A price cap increase is on the way, the latest blow to people already struggling with rising costs.
articles.body:
London, United Kingdom – Andrew, a 70-year-old retiree from the eastern English city of Norwich, had enrolled months ago in a fixed-rate energy plan for 18 months, learning from earlier price shocks caused by wars.

“I guess I saw this coming,” he told Al Jazeera.

Days ago, Ofgem, the energy regulator for England, Scotland and Wales, announced a 4 percent increase of the energy price cap from October 1, 2026, a result of the sharp rise in wholesale gas prices due to the United States-Israel war on Iran.

“The situation doesn’t look any clearer … the fog of war is still there, and who knows when it will blow away,” said Andrew, who requested that his surname be withheld for privacy.

The end of his fixed-rate plan is not something he likes to think about.

“I don’t think there’s going to be clarity,” he said. “I can’t see that the current state of geopolitics will allow for any resolution. I’m starting to think, if it’s not one conflict zone, it will be another.”

According to Ofgem, 35 percent of households in England, Scotland and Wales are on similar, fixed-rate energy plans, and will not be immediately affected by the Ofgem price cap increase.

Most, however, will face higher bills in the winter, an added blow to a nation already struggling amid a continued cost-of-living crisis.

A household using a regular level of energy will pay about 60 pounds ($80) a year more.

The UK government, alongside the increase, announced a tax cut on monthly electricity bills as part of a wider effort to shield people from the increasingly stark economic impacts of the Iran war as winter approaches. The tax cut is noted to last until the end of the 2027 financial year, but both experts and everyday people are not so sure that costs will be under control by then.

While the move on tax gives people “room to breathe, it doesn’t fix the fundamentals”, Ahmed Tabaqchali, a non-resident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told Al Jazeera.

“We are not going to see a return to normality as far as the Strait of Hormuz is concerned. One way or the other, whatever end-game with the US and Iran, there is now a change to the status quo,” said Tabaqchali, who has worked in capital markets for more than 25 years.

Volatility is not a temporary concern, he said.

“As long as the United Kingdom relies on energy imports, we are going to be impacted by geopolitics,” said Jack Burt, a PhD candidate at the University of Cambridge, researching novel forms of energy storage.

Before the Iran war, roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) passed through the Strait of Hormuz, the only route connecting the Gulf to the ocean. Iran shut the strategic waterway not long after the initial US-Israeli strikes on Tehran in late February, triggering a global energy crisis.

Shortly after those initial strikes, the UK House of Commons Library released a briefing noting that the Bank of England would likely scrap plans to lower interest rates, while predicting that household gas bills would increase.

“Higher energy costs are likely to result in the UK economic activity weakening,” the report said.

Ofgem’s move is the latest development in the ongoing energy crisis stemming from the war.

Wholesale prices have risen by 11 percent over the past three months, noted Ofgem, with Neil Kenward, the body’s director general for markets, underlining that “high international gas prices are continuing to drive energy costs in the UK”.

The price cap applies to gas and electricity, while the tax cut applies to electricity bills, meaning households that do not use gas will fare better than those that do.

While diplomatic efforts in the Gulf region have focused on keeping the Strait of Hormuz open, US attacks on Iran over the weekend – the first in a month – threaten continued destabilisation.

“The consumer is going to be paying a ‘risk premium’ for energy supply,” noted Burt.

Following the 2022 full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine, when monthly energy bills hit all-time highs, the UK moved away from gas coming through Russian pipelines “and became much more reliant on other suppliers of liquid natural gas, mostly coming from the Middle East”, he said.

Ozan, 20, a business owner in northeast London, said that “it’s getting more and more difficult to absorb the rises” for small business owners.

“Ultimately, the customer is also suffering, leading to less disposable income, meaning less spending.”

Last week, the Centre for Economics and Business Research forecast that by the end of 2027, the average UK household’s real spending power will be reduced by 2,400 pounds ($3,200), as the prices of everyday goods continue to increase.

Ofgem’s price cap will be reviewed again in January, following a quarterly schedule. But experts are predicting a continued rise in prices, painting a bleak picture for the UK’s energy sector.

Andrew, 70, is among the third of Britons locked into a deal whereby his bills will not rise for some time [Courtesy of the family]

articles.title: In 1921, Italian immigrant Simon Rodia began hand-building Los Angeles’s Watts Towers from steel, mortar and broken tile; 33 years later the construction had ended
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A small triangular lot in Los Angeles’ Watts neighborhood was purchased by Simon Rodia in 1921, who began building what would become the Watts Towers..
articles.body: A small triangular lot in Los Angeles’ Watts neighborhood was purchased by Simon Rodia in 1921, who began building what would become the Watts Towers. He worked on the site for 33 years and used steel, wire mesh and mortar, then embedded pieces of glass, tile, pottery, shells and other objects into the surfaces. The National Park Service describes the site as containing three principal towers, six smaller towers and other sculptures, walls and decorative features. The tallest tower rises 99½ feet, despite having a foundation only 14 inches deep.Rodia turned a residential lot into a building siteRodia was born in Italy in 1879 and came to the United States when he was very young. He eventually settled in California, where he worked as a laborer and tile setter before moving to Watts. He purchased the property in 1921, and the lot measured about 140 by 150 by 68 feet and included his home, garden and the structures he would build over the following decades. The National Park Service says Rodia lived and worked there until 1954.Rodia built walls and smaller decorative structures before constructing the taller towers, and also repeatedly altered sections that he had already completed, which meant the site was never simply built once and left unchanged. The National Park Service registration describes the Towers as being in a continual process of construction and reconstruction between 1921 and 1954. Rodia changed the South Wall, altered the Center Tower and transferred some of its earlier elements to the West Tower.He built the towers without weldingRodia had no equipment for welding or riveting the steel; instead, he bent lengths of steel into the shapes he wanted and tied them together with wire. He then wrapped the framework in wire mesh and applied mortar by hand. The decorative materials went into the mortar while it was being worked, and the surfaces contain pieces of glass, shells and other objects, along with tile and pottery. The Library of Congress describes the construction as steel pipes and rods wrapped in wire mesh and coated with mortar, with porcelain, tile, glass and found objects incorporated into the finished structures.The National Park Service says he did not use ladders or scaffolding when building the tallest tower; rather, he waited for sections of cement to harden and used the horizontal rings around the structure as footholds. The West Tower was the tallest of the three principal towers, and reaches 99 1⁄2 feet, with its foundation only 14 inches deep. The Center Tower measures 97 feet 10 inches, while the East Tower reaches 55 feet and was the first of the three large towers Rodia constructed.Glass, pottery and shells became part of the wallsRodia used materials that were available to him rather than relying on a conventional architectural finish, such as pieces of pottery, colorful glass, shells, tile and other objects pressed into the mortar throughout the site. The National Park Service records decorated walls containing pottery shards, glass and other objects. One section includes rows of objects shaped like corncobs and boots, while the gazebo contains tiles, seashells, pottery and pieces of colored glass.The site also includes a structure known as the “Ship of Marco Polo,” a gazebo, fountains, decorated walls and smaller sculptures. The three main towers are connected visually and structurally with other elements across the property. California State Parks describes the Watts Towers as a work of architectural sculpture made from a steel core wrapped in wire mesh and covered with mortar, with tile, glass, shell, pottery and rocks embedded into the surface.Rodia left Watts in 1954Rodia gave the house, garden and Towers to a neighbor when he was in his mid-70s in 1954 and moved to Northern California. He never returned to Watts, and his house burned the following year. The National Park Service records that the fire destroyed the building but left part of its decorated facade, posts, fireplace and chimney.Los Angeles officials later considered demolishing the property because of concerns about their structural safety. A preservation campaign formed to oppose the demolition, and in 1959, an engineering test subjected the tallest Towers to forces intended to simulate severe wind conditions. The test equipment failed before the structures did, which helped preservationists make their case for keeping the site.The Towers became a protected landmarkThe Watts Towers were entered into the National Register of Historic Places in 1977, and the National Park Service listing identifies 1921 and 1954 as significant years for the property and records the site at 1765 East 107th Street in Los Angeles. California State Parks now describes the site as a National Historic Landmark and notes that it is operated by Los Angeles County. The tallest tower remains 99½ feet high, and the structures still stand on the original Watts property. The Library of Congress has also documented the Towers in its photographic collections, and its records identify the structures as the work of Italian immigrant construction worker Sabato Rodia and note that he built them between 1921 and 1954 using steel, wire mesh, mortar, and embedded decorative objects.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Russian drone and missile barrage kills at least 12 in Ukraine’s Kyiv
articles.summary: Russian attacks escalate as EU defence ministers meet in Ireland to discuss Ukraine air defence shortages.
articles.body:
At least 12 people have been killed and 21 wounded in a wave of Russian air attacks on Ukraine’s capital Kyiv and the surrounding region, authorities said.

“Kyiv region came under a massive attack by Russian missiles and strike drones tonight,” Kyiv regional military administration chief Tymur Tkachenko said on Telegram on Tuesday.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy denounced “Russian terror” and said an Indian citizen was among the dead, calling on allies to boost Ukraine’s air defences.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said at least eight people were killed and five others, including two children, were injured during the overnight drone and missile attacks on the city.

Another four people were killed in the Kyiv region, Ukrainian prosecutors announced, saying a residential building was damaged in the suburb of Boryspil.

Zelenskyy said 50 people were evacuated from the building in Boryspil.

“Russia always plans its strikes specifically to cause as much destruction to people’s lives as possible, and it succeeds only when air defence capabilities are insufficient,” he said on social media.

Russia’s Ministry of Defence said it hit military ⁠and energy facilities ⁠in Kyiv and Odesa, ‌as well as regions surrounding these cities overnight.

Ukraine’s border service also said Russian forces hit the ferry checkpoint at Orlivka on the border with Romania, a NATO member.

⁠Ukraine’s air force spokesman Yurii Ihnat said Russia was launching drones that were harder to shoot down. In the last six days, 2,800 jet-powered drones had been launched at Ukraine, with only 60 percent intercepted.

Reporting from Kyiv, Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine said Russia’s tactic of launching continuous waves of drones during the day was aimed at disrupting civilian life.

“Every time there’s an air raid siren, people have to evacuate certain commercial buildings and schools have to go underground. Ninety percent of Ukraine’s modern food storage has been destroyed, so grocery stores are having fewer supplies,” MacAlpine said.

In Russia, a Ukrainian drone attack caused a ⁠fire in the port area of Ust-Luga, a major export outlet in the northwest, and ⁠Moscow was repelling drones.

In the Samara region, a Ukrainian drone attack hit the town of Novokuibyshevsk, blowing out windows in an apartment building, Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said on Telegram.

Novokuibyshevsk and the surrounding ⁠area on the ⁠Volga River are home to a ⁠number of ⁠Russia’s major ⁠oil refineries run by the state ‌oil company Rosneft.

The acting governor of Russia’s Belgorod region said a Ukrainian attack killed one person.

Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately attacking civilians.

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s drone forces commander says it hit 54 Russian “shadow fleet” vessels in August to prevent oil sales funding Russia’s war in Ukraine.

The attacks come as European Union defence and foreign ministers gather in Ireland for talks on strengthening Ukraine’s air defences.

Ukraine faces a shortage of interceptor missiles, particularly United States-made Patriot systems used against ballistic threats.

Both sides have escalated long-range strikes in recent months, hitting infrastructure such as warehouses, businesses, and oil and port facilities, as well as ships, increasing civilian casualties.

articles.title: MORNING GLORY: We're living through the Summer of the DSA (and Hasan Piker)
articles.summary: The DSA's march through Democratic primaries and Hasan Piker's radical rhetoric could reshape the 2026 midterms into a choice election for voters.
articles.body: 1967’s "Summer of Love" kicked off the American habit of defining a summer season with a phrase. Some phrases stick. Some do not. 1968’s "Summer of Rage" tagline stuck. The "Summer of Watergate" could be 1973 and the Senate Select Committee’s hearings would have stuck, but President Richard Nixon survived those and would have survived the summer of 1974 but for the release of the tapes. MORNING GLORY: HASAN PIKER’S RADICAL RHETORIC IS BECOMING DEMOCRATS’ 2026 BRAND The Bicentennial Summer was as memorable as this summer’s celebration of the 250th birthday of the United States — but those months are defined by a day, not months. 1977’s Summer of Sam, 1994’s Summer of O.J. and 2020’s Summer of George Floyd are not fixtures of the language, but do serve as reference points. With a week left in this summer, the touchpoints seem likely to be the rise of Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and the meteoric rise in awareness among the general public of Hasan Piker, an online Twitch streamer whose toxic combination of radical politics, profanity, vulgarity, anti-Israel and hate-filled rhetoric merged with the DSA’s march through the Democratic primaries to make it appear to "normal" Americans from the center-left to the center-right as though the Democratic Party had become unhinged and taken over by a cult-like group of crazed anti-American extremists. The "Summer of the DSA and Hasan Piker" is unwieldy, but accurate. Shorthand will probably reduce it to the "Summer of the DSA," and even though Piker is closely ideologically aligned with DSA, appearing at DSA events and rallies, Piker does not appear to be a dues-paying DSAer. Still, the "Summer of DSA" will catch him up even as it includes the primary election victories of Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania, Claire Valdez, Darializa Avila Chevalier and Brad Lander in New York (Lander is a former DSA member but left in 2023), and Democratic Senate nominees Angie Nixon in Florida and Troy Jackson in Maine who are DSA-endorsed candidates. Hard-left "progressive" Democrats running for Senate like Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, Sherrod Brown in Ohio and James Talarico in Texas have not been formally endorsed by their state DSAs or the national group, but their ascendancy compliments rather than contradicts the enormous shift to the left of the Democrats in the wake of President Trump’s re-election in 2024. DSA’S GROWING GRIP ON DEM PARTY HITS NEW TERRITORY AS ESTABLISHMENT FALLS IN LINE Will the "Summer of DSA" define the actual midterms ahead? Many in legacy media want to define the fall’s voting, which culminates on November 3, as a referendum on President Trump but that’s not what is unfolding. The rise of the DSA and unhinged rantings like those of Piker as well as numerous "co-chairs" of the DSA has muddied what would typically be a "referendum" election, turning it in many if not most statewide or Congressional district races into a "choice election" of the sort Republicans are hoping for. Because the DSA, Piker, candidates like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and James Talarico in Texas are just so far outside of the mainstream of American politics as to shift the awareness of the American electorate away from the issues of 2026 to the much bigger issue of the future of the country. The vast majority of Americans love their country. They can and do disagree among themselves on the politics of the moment and the policies that would best serve the country’s future. MARK HALPERIN CALLS HASAN PIKER A 'HORRIBLE PERSON' AS DEMOCRATS FACE PRESSURE TO DISTANCE FROM STREAMER But, that they want a future similar to the past, but improved at the margins remains the central and abiding truth of the American experience. We don’t want the "DSA way" and we sure do not want people addicted to rage the way Hasan Piker is to dominate our politics. El-Sayed’s limp attempt to distance himself from Piker this past weekend as summer draws to a close only guaranteed another week or more of scrutiny on El-Sayed’s choice to bring Piker into the Wolverine State’s politics. El-Sayed put on the Piker bodysuit, and it turns out it is very difficult if not impossible to erase that choice from the electorate’s consciousness. The Squad is almost certainly going to control the choice of the next House Democratic Leader. The increase in "Squad" numbers may remove Hakeem Jeffries as Leader of House Democrats, but it may not. Republicans are well aware of what a small majority means: the empowerment of the party’s fringiest members. The DSA could well be running the next House majority. DEMOCRATS NO LONGER HAVE THE NO. 1 WEAPON TO KEEP THEIR SOCIALIST WING IN LINE The "Summer of the DSA" has made that possibility a crucial issue across every federal race. It is not a cause for celebration among Republicans, who realize that the country needs a healthy Democratic Party and not one run by extremists from the left. Democrats need a way back to "between the '30s" competition in American political debates or the Democrats could face a wipeout of their extremist candidates outside of deep blue Congressional districts. (A "between the ‘40s" field would be even better for them.) An electoral train wreck in 2026 would, however, prevent an even worse crack-up in 2028, a presidential election year that could become a replay of the 1972 crash-out of the Democrats under the banner of George McGovern. articles.title: Trump says Iran is ‘DEAD’ — experts point to the real sign Tehran is nearing the brink
articles.summary: U.S. strikes on Iranian launchers near the Strait of Hormuz triggered ballistic missile retaliation as Brent crude climbed above $90 a barrel Monday.
articles.body: President Donald Trump declared Iran a "Failed Nation" Monday, claiming the country is economically and militarily broken as renewed fighting with the U.S. raises questions about how much leverage Tehran still has left. "Iran is officially a Failed Nation. IT IS DEAD!" Trump wrote on Truth Social Monday morning. "They have no Navy, they have no Air Force, they have no currency, they are not paying their soldiers or police." Trump also claimed Iranian inflation had reached 300% and said the country's leadership was "in total disarray and incapable of properly representing the country." Iran is facing pressure from nearly every direction — renewed U.S. military strikes, tighter sanctions and a steep drop in oil exports — raising fresh questions about how long Tehran can keep absorbing the economic pain and still maintain leverage against Washington. COULD IRAN’S REGIME COLLAPSE? EXPERTS ASSESS BESSENT’S BID TO SEVER FINANCIAL LIFELINES Official Iranian data cited by Reuters put annual inflation at 66% in July, while the IMF projects average consumer-price inflation of 68.9% in 2026. Trump's post came amid the sharpest U.S.-Iran military escalation in weeks. U.S. forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island Sunday after Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz, according to a U.S. official. Iran retaliated by launching ballistic missiles toward U.S. bases in Jordan, while Jordan said it intercepted eight missiles that entered its airspace. The renewed confrontation comes as Washington ratchets up economic pressure. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Reuters Sunday that the administration expects to roll out additional secondary sanctions as frequently as every week, initially focusing on banks and potentially cutting financial institutions that continue facilitating Iranian transactions out of the U.S. dollar-based financial system. IRAN’S DEEPEST WEAKNESS IS GETTING EXPOSED THROUGH AMERICA’S MAXIMUM PRESSURE CAMPAIGN Iran's own leaders are acknowledging growing economic strain. President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran's exports and imports have fallen nearly 35% because of U.S. sanctions and the naval blockade, while annual inflation reached 66% in July, Reuters reported Aug. 29. The IMF projects Iran's economy will contract 5.4% this year. Miad Maleki, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies who previously served as associate director of Treasury's Office of Global Targeting at the Office of Foreign Assets Control, told Fox News Digital that the Islamic Republic may be nearing an economic breaking point. FDD says Maleki previously helped oversee U.S. sanctions programs and served as chief and senior sanctions coordinator for Iran and the Middle East. "I think where we stand today, it's very clear — we see very clear signs, indications of what I would call an economy that is on the verge of collapse, if it hasn't already collapsed yet," Maleki said. Maleki argued that the critical pressure point is Iran's ability to turn oil exports into usable revenue. US TARGETS CHINESE REFINERY IN SWEEPING IRAN OIL CRACKDOWN, SANCTIONS ‘SHADOW FLEET’ TANKERS He estimates Tehran needs roughly 1 million barrels of oil exports per day to sustain itself, about 1.5 million to avoid hyperinflation and approximately 2 million to support development. Maleki said Iranian exports have fallen dramatically and Tehran is increasingly struggling to repatriate revenue from the oil it can sell. Kpler data cited by Reuters showed Chinese imports of Iranian crude falling from an average 1.4 million barrels per day in 2025 to a provisional 534,000 barrels per day so far in August. Maleki said Tehran is increasingly relying on money creation rather than cutting politically sensitive salaries and pensions. But there are limits. "They can keep printing money, but they can't really print the type of commodities that they need, such as gasoline, such as wheat," he said. The pressure, however, may create a dangerous paradox. IRAN COULD UNLEASH ‘KINETIC’ RESPONSE AS US TIGHTENS ECONOMIC CONTAINMENT, ANALYST WARNS Iran analyst Danny Citrinowicz, a fellow at Israel's Institute for National Security Studies and a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council's Scowcroft Middle East Security Initiative, told Fox News Digital that the maritime blockade, wartime losses and wider economic pressure are hurting Tehran, but argued Washington should not assume economic pain will lead to capitulation. Citrinowicz said continued pressure could instead increase Tehran's incentive to escalate if Iranian leaders conclude the status quo is worse than renewed confrontation. He said Iran could attempt to target "U.S. economic assets in the Gulf," ports or U.S. vessels involved in enforcing the blockade, even as its missile-production capabilities have been degraded. Maleki agreed Iran would likely attempt to escalate, but questioned how much leverage Tehran still possesses. "They're going to try to escalate," Maleki said, pointing to the attacks of the last 24 hours. But he argued that further escalation would increasingly affect Gulf states Iran has relied upon for trade, sanctions evasion and diplomacy — potentially bringing even greater economic and diplomatic pressure. MILLIONS OF BARRELS OF IRANIAN OIL SIT BEYOND TRUMP BLOCKADE AS HE VOWS ‘ZERO LEAKAGE’ Asked whether Iran was losing its leverage, Maleki responded: "Absolutely." He argued Tehran has emerged weakened from internal unrest and the external war and is increasingly isolated domestically and internationally. What Maleki is watching next is not necessarily missed government payrolls, but shortages that could trigger another wave of domestic unrest. "What I'm looking for is shortages of items such as gasoline," Maleki said. "Right now they're fighting a war inside Iran that is way more challenging to the regime than it is from external forces that they're facing." Commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remained severely disrupted Monday, while Brent crude climbed more than 2% to above $90 as markets reacted to the renewed U.S.-Iran exchanges. Reuters reported Aug. 31 that Gulf oil flows have recovered from their wartime lows but remain below pre-war levels. Maleki said he expects Iranians to return to the streets and argued Western governments should prepare now to help them communicate and organize if Tehran again shuts down internet access. "What we need to do is to contain this regime, cut off this economic lifeline, empower the Iranian people, be prepared next time Iranians are back on the street [and] take actions to stop this regime from slaughtering Iranians," Maleki said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Those are the right policies — put the pressure on, be prepared to push back on the Iranian regime every time it escalates," he added. "At this point, they are the weakest they've been since 1979. Every time they try to escalate, they become weaker." Reuters contributed to this story.
