articles.title: Smell of death hangs over rescue efforts in Nepal as deaths pass 1,000
articles.summary: The overwhelming stench of death is crushing hopes that more survivors will be found in this Nepalese town devastated by last week’s catastrophic floods.
articles.body: BIDUR, Nepal — The overwhelming stench of death is crushing hopes that more survivors will be found in this Nepalese town devastated by last week’s catastrophic floods. Workers in white hazmat suits unload bodies from a stream of ambulances in Bidur, a town in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on Tuesday. They place the wrapped bodies onto blue tarp in a cordoned off area. Helicopters, both military and civilian aircraft that in better days would be used for commercial tours, take off packed with aid before returning with survivors in need of medical care. Kalpana Shrestha, a nurse who works in capital Kathmandu, is desperate. Ten members of her family are missing — her two sisters and their children — are missing. “I have shared their photos with journalists, on social media and YouTube but I have not got any response at all,” she said speaking with NBC News in Kathmandu. She added that her loved ones disappeared in Betrawati, a town some 60 miles from the capital that was obliterated in the flooding. “I have posted so much that my fingers started shaking and trembling,” said Shrestha, 35. “My mind has stopped working. But even so, we have not stopped posting.” More than 1,000 have been declared dead in Nepal after last week’s devastating floods, according to Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. Over 3,915 others are still missing, including at least 583 foreign nationals. In Tibet, at least 16 people were killed and 546 are missing, according to CGTN, China’s English-language satellite news channel. At least 80 Americans are among the missing in Nepal. More than 10,000 people have been rescued so far, including 252 foreign nationals, the United Nations says. The disaster, which was triggered by a glacier collapse and landslide on Nepal’s border with China, is now considered Nepal’s deadliest natural disaster since the April 2015 earthquake that killed around 9,000 people in Nepal. Shrestha said she felt that the government was “not doing enough work to search and rescue to locate” her family. She also noted that access to her village was still difficult after the floods. “Our brothers did try but failed to reach them and had to return home,” she said. “The road is gone, there is no access at all.” Access remains the single biggest obstacle to response efforts, with roads passable only as far as Nuwakot and some sections of highway linking Kathmandu to the hardest areas still completely blocked, according to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs. And the bodies that have been recovered pose a huge challenge to authorities, who are using at least 21 hospitals in a string of districts to store remains, according to Nepal’s disaster agency. In some cases, bodies are being buried to prevent any risk of infection, with hopes they will be later identified so the remains can be returned to loved ones. Speaking with NBC News in Pokhara, Nabin Karki, a superintendent of police, said authorities were collecting DNA samples and display photos of the bodies found so in hopes that family members might be able to identify them. Relatives of those missing can provide blood samples for DNA testing, he said, and if a match is found the body can be taken from the burial site and handed over to the family for a funeral. Janis Mackey Frayer and Dawn Liu reported from Bidur, Nepal. Michael Fiorentino and Surendra Phuyal reported from Kathmandu, Nepal. Sunil Pandey reported from Pokhara, Nepal.

articles.title: New York Times Square stabbing: Who is Pamela Cisneros? Woman behind attack had mental health history
articles.summary: US News: A 49-year-old Queens woman identified as Pamela Cisneros was fatally shot by New York police after she allegedly stabbed two people in a random and un.
articles.body: A 49-year-old Queens woman identified as Pamela Cisneros was fatally shot by New York police after she allegedly stabbed two people in a random and unprovoked attack in the heart of Times Square. Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said Cisneros had a documented mental-health history with the NYPD, including incidents in 2018 and 2019, but had no arrest history. The attack unfolded on Monday afternoon when Cisneros allegedly pulled two large knives from a shopping bag and stabbed a 68-year-old man and, moments later, a 32-year-old woman. The woman later died at Bellevue Hospital, while the man remained in stable condition. Police then confronted Cisneros, who refused repeated orders to drop the knives before officers fatally shot her.Who was Pamela Cisneros?Pamela Cisneros was a 49-year-old woman from Queens who was identified by the NYPD as the suspect in the Times Square double stabbing. Authorities have not released extensive biographical information about her, and the circumstances surrounding her life before the attack remain limited in the public record. What police have confirmed is that Cisneros had previous documented interactions with the NYPD connected to mental-health concerns. Commissioner Jessica Tisch said those incidents occurred in 2018 and 2019, while also stressing that Cisneros had no arrest history with the department.What happened in Times Square?The incident began shortly after 4:20pm near West 41st Street and Seventh Avenue, according to police. Tisch said Cisneros took two knives from a red shopping bag and approached a 68-year-old man who had just left a subway station and was waiting to cross the street with his wife. She allegedly stabbed him in the abdomen before moving north along Seventh Avenue and attacking a 32-year-old woman in the abdomen. The two stabbings occurred within about 20 seconds of each other. Both victims were taken to Bellevue Hospital, where the woman was pronounced dead. The male victim remained in stable condition.Police confronted Cisneros with two knivesWitnesses alerted officers after the attacks, and police encountered Cisneros on Seventh Avenue between West 42nd and West 43rd streets. Tisch said officers spent about four minutes speaking to her and repeatedly ordered her to drop the knives. She refused to comply and, according to the commissioner, told officers, “I’m not dropping anything. I would rather kill both of you.” She reportedly repeated a threat to kill the officers as the confrontation continued. Body-camera footage captured the encounter, according to police, and officials said the footage will be released.Why did police shoot her?Police said officers tried to stop Cisneros without immediately resorting to gunfire. Multiple officers deployed Tasers, but the devices failed to incapacitate her. Video described by authorities showed Cisneros continuing towards officers while holding and waving the knives. Two officers then fired their service weapons, striking Cisneros. She was taken to Bellevue Hospital, where she was pronounced dead. The police shooting is being investigated, as is standard in officer-involved shootings, while Tisch and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani defended the officers' response and said their actions prevented the situation from becoming even more serious.What is known about her mental health history?Tisch said Cisneros had a documented mental-health history with the NYPD and had been involved in incidents with police in 2018 and 2019. The commissioner did not provide further details about those incidents or identify a specific diagnosis. Authorities also said Cisneros had no previous arrest history with the department. The disclosure has become a significant part of the investigation because police described the Times Square attacks as random and unprovoked, while officials characterised Cisneros as emotionally disturbed. However, there is currently no public evidence establishing a specific motive for the stabbings or directly explaining how her previous mental-health contacts related to Monday's attack.Was the Times Square attack terrorism?Police said there was no evidence at this stage suggesting that the attack was terrorism-related. Tisch described the stabbings as random and unprovoked, with the victims apparently selected without any known connection to Cisneros. The attack took place in one of New York City's busiest tourist areas and near an NYPD substation, making the rapid police response particularly significant. Investigators are continuing to examine the circumstances surrounding the stabbings, the police confrontation and the fatal shooting.The investigation will now focus on reconstructing the sequence of events, including the two stabbings, the four-minute confrontation and the moment officers opened fire. Police said the shooting was captured on body-worn cameras, which could provide investigators with a detailed account of the officers' commands, Cisneros's movements and the failed attempts to subdue her. The identities of the two stabbing victims had not initially been released pending notification of their families. Meanwhile, authorities are expected to examine Cisneros's previous interactions with police and any other information that could shed light on what led to the seemingly random attack in Times Square.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Rescued turtle cared for in Weymouth to be released in the Azores
articles.summary: Crush the loggerhead turtle will be released into the Atlantic along with two other rescued turtles.
articles.body:
A rare turtle that was flown to the UK after being rescued in Jersey has been transported to the Azores, along with two others, where they will be released later.

The loggerhead turtle, named Crush by her rescuers, was found lifeless on a beach on 19 January following Storm Goretti.

Malnourished and suffering from hypothermia, she was flown to Southampton and transferred to Weymouth Sea Life centre where she has been cared for by experts.

After a period back in quarantine, Crush has been flown 1,500 miles (2,500km) to the Azores, along with fellow loggerheads Eden and Tiree who were rescued on the west coast of Scotland in 2025.

Eden was found on a beach at Troon, in October and has been cared for at Brighton Sea Life, while Tiree - named after the island where she was found in November - was cared for alongside Crush in Weymouth.

Throughout Crush's rehabilitation, the team at Weymouth remained in constant contact with vets at International Zoo Veterinary Group (IZVG) to monitor her health.

Kico Iraola, curator at Sea Life Weymouth said: "Both Tiree and Crush were very poorly little turtles when they came to us here at Weymouth.

"We initially raised their temperature to bring them out of cold shock, and they underwent a series of routine blood tests, X-rays and CT scans before being deemed fit for release.

"We have really enjoyed seeing them grow and come back to full health and now to embark on the next stage of their adventure."

Sea Life Brighton has the UK's first permanent rehabilitation centre dedicated exclusively to sea turtle recovery.

Joe Williams, curator at Sea Life Brighton, said: "Though it's sad to wave Eden goodbye, we feel full of joy for her to leave us and continue growing up, and to be part of this vulnerable species' conservation efforts."

Crush's recovery has also been supported by Jersey marine charity Littlefeet Environmental, which has provided a satellite transmitter to track her after her release.

Chairman Andrew Farmer said: "This will allow us to fill vital data gaps on sea turtle migratory corridors in the North Atlantic."

When Crush was found by a dog walker, she was cold-stunned - a hypothermia-like condition that causes the turtle's body to shut down.

She was initially cared for by New Era Veterinary Hospital in Jersey, including two weeks at clinical director Peter Hawarth's family home, before he flew to Southampton, carrying her in a box .

Loggerhead turtles can be found in the subtropical waters off north Africa and it is believed Crush was swept north by storms and currents.

Others have been found in Sussex, Suffolk and as far north as Tyree in Scotland.

The species is classed as "vulnerable" on the IUCN Red List. There are an estimated 2,000 breeding females worldwide and out of every 1,000 hatchlings, on average, only one makes it to adulthood.

It is not known if Crush is female but rescuers called her "she" because, like other females, she has a larger tail.

articles.title: Liberals sweep three seats in boost for Carney after trade tensions with US
articles.summary: One seat was taken from the Conservatives, indicating public support for the PM after a confrontation with Donald Trump.
articles.body:
Mark Carney's Liberal Party won all three parliamentary special elections that were held in Canada on Monday, indicating ongoing public support for the prime minister well into his second year in office and after recent trade tensions with the US.

The votes were triggered by the resignations of three MPs. The most notable result saw Carney's party claim a Québec seat previously held by an opposition Conservative.

In the other two votes, in Ontario and British Columbia, the Liberals held onto their seats as pollsters expected.

Carney has received a bump in the polls following his decision to end trade talks with the US, accusing Canada's southern neighbour of proposing terms that were "unfair".

The prime minister congratulated the three victorious Liberal candidates in a post on X. Reflecting on the wider issues facing his premiership, he wrote: "Canada is being tested in a changing world, and Canadians are up for it."

The results mean Carney will keep his slim majority in the House of Commons.

Canadian media projected a sizeable victory for the Liberals in the Québec district of Chicoutimi-Le Fjord. Liberal candidate Daniel Gobeil, a dairy farmer, becomes the district's new MP, having claimed more than half of the overall vote.

He beat the Bloc Québécois and the Conservatives into second and third places respectively. The seat had been a narrow three-way race last time round.

Addressing his supporters in French, Gobeil said "this victory means we can maintain Canadian unity all across the country", CBC reported.

Elsewhere, Tanveer Shahnawaz won his contest in Beaches-East York, Ontario, and Braeden Caley emerged victorious from the race in North Vancouver-Capilano, British Columbia.

The Conservatives have struggled to close the gap with the Liberals since losing last year's federal election, with the latest polls suggesting they are trailing behind Carney's party by about 10 points.

Four members of their ranks crossed the floor to the governing Liberals since the April 2025 election, and three others have either resigned or have announced plans to do so.

Richard Martel, the former Conservative MP of the Quebec constituency that held Monday's by-election, stepped down last month after he was appointed by Carney to Canada's Senate. Senators in Canada are not elected.

The loss of Martel's seat to the Liberals is another blow to Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre, who won a leadership test in January by a landslide but has faced questions about his ability to navigate the current political climate in Canada.

Meanwhile, the approval of Carney's government rose four points in recent weeks, as has the prime minister's personal popularity, according to figures released on Monday by Canadian pollster Abacus Data .

David Coletto, founder of Abacus Data, credits this boost to US President Donald Trump's lack of popularity with Canadians, as well as the country rallying around Carney's decision to walk away from trade talks with the White House.

This trend is most pronounced in Quebec, Coletto wrote in a note on Monday, where "Carney's personal rating is stronger there than anywhere else in the country".

Quebec stands to be one of the most provinces most affected by Trump's new 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods, which came into effect after trade talks collapsed earlier this month.

In a recent report, global forecasting firm Oxford Economics warned that Quebec could lose C$2bn ($1.4bn; £1bn) in annual output by 2028.

articles.title: A brutal summer just got worse for the 49ers and they don't have an answer for it
articles.summary: Aaron Donald's NFL comeback with the Rams adds to a brutal San Francisco 49ers summer already marred by Kyle Shanahan's car crash and injuries.
articles.body: It's hard to find an NFL team that has had a worse summer than the San Francisco 49ers. And it just got worse. The 49ers, an otherwise good team, have for the past couple of months been weaving and slipping bad news like a boxer trying to avoid a knockout punch. Remember that head coach Kyle Shanahan in July got into a terrible head-on collision that he actually caused when he went looking for his cell phone in his car while relying on his Tesla's autopilot feature to drive for him. 49ERS COACH KYLE SHANAHAN ADMITS HE CAUSED CAR CRASH AFTER TAKING EYES OFF ROAD TO FIND HIS PHONE The ensuing head-on collision when his car drifted into an oncoming lane left Shanahan with broken bones, facial lacerations, a concussion and regrets. And, amazingly, that was perhaps the least bit of football-related bad news the team got during training camp. Because ... Defensive end Nick Bosa, trying to get ready for the regular season after ACL surgery last season, hasn't practiced in four weeks and is not ready to play. Tight end George Kittle, trying to get ready for the season after surgery to repair a torn Achilles, hasn't practiced during training camp either, despite constant reports he's on the mend and ahead of schedule. Then majority owner Jed York got popped in a prostitution sting by the Mahoning Valley Human Trafficking Task Force in Ohio. The arrest and York subsequently pleading no contest to lesser charges didn't stop the story from going viral and putting York in the crosshairs of the NFL Personal Conduct Policy. Hey, um, did we mention that 2024 first-round pick Ricky Pearsall, required knee surgery the first week of August, effectively ending his 2026 season before it even began? Breaking: None of this is good. MORE DETAILS FROM JED YORK ARREST DURING PROSTITUTION STING But it gets potentially worse. On Sunday, Aaron Donald announced he is returning to the NFL to play for the Los Angeles Rams after being retired the past two years. Donald saw what the Rams have done this offseason in loading up for a run at the Super Bowl and decided he wanted to join the fun and make life difficult for rivals like ... the 49ers. And although the three-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year has been out since 2024, Donald thinks he's still going to be dang good at age 35. During his comeback news conference Donald detailed his grueling preparation to return to the game. He said he ran full-speed on the treadmill and lifted weights to stay in top physical shape during his time away from the game. And he explained that he worked with the trainer who had known him since high school to get an honest assessment of his current explosiveness compared to that of his youth. "You ain't missed a step," Donald said his private trainer told him. That's great for the Rams. But not so much for the 49ers because they play the Rams twice in the NFC West, including in their season opener Sept. 10 in Australia. More bad news? Of course. Shanahan on Monday announced he doesn't know who is going to start at left guard in that game to fill the assignment of blocking Donald. "Don't know yet," Shanahan told reporters when asked for details. The 49ers practiced Monday, then will do so again Tuesday and Wednesday before leaving for Australia. And until those practices happen, well, Shanahan isn't ready to pick a starter. "We haven't had those three practices yet and we just added a new guy to the group too," the coach said. "So, it's truly fluid." This isn't a coach being coy about an answer he doesn't want to reveal for competitive purposes. This feels more like Shanahan and his staff evaluated rookie fourth-round pick Carver Willis throughout training camp and do not feel comfortable enough to name him as the starter. And definitely not against Aaron Donald. CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM The 49ers were so uncertain about Carver they felt compelled to trade for depth-guy Jarrett Patterson in an exchange with the Houston Texans. And now the depth guy they acquired is suddenly in the mix to start less than two days after joining the team. "It's still fluid in all our positions in there, so I want to see where he fits in the group in these three days," Shanahan said. "So, I want to get him in the group, see where he fits, just see him in person, see how he can help us at guard, how he can help us at center and how he stacks up to the other guys." It's not all terrible news for the 49ers. The NFL has given Donald a roster exemption in case the Rams feel he needs more ramp-up time before playing again. That could mean he doesn't play the 49ers in that season-opener. Sure, Aaron Donald might decide after spending six weeks getting ready for his NFL return, it would be wise to not play in a nationally televised game against a rookie or a guy the 49ers just added to the roster. The body of a 46-year-old man was recovered Sunday. Officials have not released his name. The recovery of a second body was announced Monday. Texas chiropractor John Giusti, 46, died in the flood, his family and the families of two others said. In July 2025, the Dragon Bravo megafire charred nearly 150,000 acres at Grand Canyon National Park. In February, the park started reopening the North Kaibab Trail, a route that connects the canyon’s North Rim with Phantom Ranch, a lodge inside the park. That same month, the National Park Service warned that the megafire had left parts of the North Rim more vulnerable to sudden, destructive rushes of water. It’s still unclear how much the Dragon Bravo fire contributed to Saturday’s floods. Although the burn zone is upstream of the spot where flooding was most severe, the fire stripped away vegetation that might otherwise have slowed rainwater, said Tom Martin, who has researched the Grand Canyon for decades. As the world warms, these types of snowballing hazards — drought that raises the risk of fire, which in turn primes hills for landslides and floods, for example — are a growing problem in the western U.S. and around the world. articles.title: No pint-sized matter: Thieves steal $70,000 in Pabst beer from California warehouse
articles.summary: MONTCLAIR, Calif.
articles.body: MONTCLAIR, Calif. — Thieves made off with tens of thousands of cans of Pabst beer in two separate heists from a Southern California warehouse on the same day, police said. Pabst Blue Ribbon has turned the thefts — valued by police at $70,000 — into a light-hearted social media promotion. But police in Montclair said Friday that investigators are trying to determine whether they were part of a single operation. In the first heist, about $45,000 worth of beer headed to Tucson, Arizona, was picked up but never delivered, according to police. An hour later, a “purported subcontracting company” submitted fake documents to pick up another $25,000 worth of beer, Montclair police said in a news release. Both thefts occurred on Aug. 17 at an Anheuser-Busch distribution center about 40 miles (65 kilometers) east of Los Angeles. Roughly 34,000 cans of Pabst Blue Ribbon and non-alcoholic Old Milwaukee beer — more than 1,500 cases — were stolen, according to a police report obtained by the Los Angeles Times. In Instagram posts, Pabst put the weight of the stolen cargo at 40,000 pounds (18,145 kilograms) and started a countdown seeking its return. “To the thief: we don’t fault you for wanting to brag to your friends how much PBR you have, we just wish you obtained it the honorable way,” the company wrote. It added, “P.s. this is real and we are deadly serious.”

articles.title: Keir Starmer announces he is standing down as MP
articles.summary: The former prime minister said he would now turn his focus to international affairs.
articles.body:
Sir Keir Starmer has announced he is to stand down as MP for Holborn and St Pancras, a move that will trigger a by-election in the London seat.

In a statement to the Camden New Journal newspaper, he said it had been a "huge honour and privilege" to represent the constituency for 11 years but he would now turn his focus to "international affairs".

Sir Keir stood down as prime minister earlier in the summer, with Andy Burnham replacing him.

It follows weeks of speculation about whether Sir Keir would remain as MP following his resignation.

In a BBC interview shortly after stepping down as PM, Sir Keir said he would stay as an MP until the next general election.

But in his statement released on Tuesday, Sir Keir said he was ready to "pass the baton to a successor".

He added: "I will now focus on other things and that will be international affairs including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world.

"I will also continue, as I have done for a long time now with others, to work on combating violence against women and girls; that is an issue that matters to me hugely.

"It's work I started before I became an MP and it's work I'm keen to continue after I'm an MP. So international affairs on the one hand, and continuing my work on violence against women and girls on the other."

articles.title: 12,000-year-old skeletons buried in an embrace in Italy were women, with ancient DNA revealing a mother-daughter link and rare genetic disease
articles.summary: Europe News: In 1963, archaeologists exploring Romito Cave in Calabria, southern Italy, uncovered an unusual Upper Palaeolithic burial in which two people lay toge.
articles.body: In 1963, archaeologists exploring Romito Cave in Calabria, southern Italy, uncovered an unusual Upper Palaeolithic burial in which two people lay together in an embrace more than 12,000 years ago. For decades, the remains were believed to belong to an adult male and an adolescent male, with their differences in body size adding to questions about their identity and relationship. As per Sapienza University of Rome, researchers found that both individuals were female and were first-degree relatives, most likely a mother and daughter. The genetic evidence also helped solve a long-standing medical mystery surrounding the younger individual, revealing a rare inherited disorder linked to the NPR2 gene. The discovery not only changes the identity of the two prehistoric individuals but also provides clues about genetic disease in ancient populations.What did researchers discover about the two skeletons buried in Romito CaveThe two skeletons were discovered together in Romito Cave, a Palaeolithic site in Calabria, in 1963. The unusual burial drew attention because the individuals had been laid to rest in an embrace. One skeleton, known as Romito 1, belonged to an adult who stood about 145 centimetres tall, while Romito 2 was an adolescent measuring around 110 centimetres. Earlier assessments identified both individuals as male, but their sex and relationship remained uncertain. The striking difference in their stature, particularly the smaller size of Romito 2, also raised the possibility of a rare skeletal disorder. Researchers have now revisited the remains using ancient DNA recovered from the inner ear, an area known to preserve genetic material particularly well over thousands of years.What does DNA reveal about the two Romito Cave skeletonsGenetic testing changed the interpretation of the burial. DNA analysis established that Romito 1 and Romito 2 were both female and that they were first-degree relatives, most likely a mother and daughter. This finding means the embrace was not the burial of an adult man and adolescent boy, as previously believed. Researchers examined their genetic connection while investigating the unusual physical features seen in their skeletons. Romito 2 carried two copies of a variant in the NPR2 gene, while the older woman carried one altered copy. The new results clarify that the two individuals were biologically related, rather than simply members of the same burial group.What rare genetic disease was identified in the 12,000-year-old adolescentThe genetic results provided the first DNA-confirmed diagnosis of a rare disease in a person who lived more than 12,000 years ago. Romito 2 had two copies of an NPR2 variant, confirming Maroteaux-type acromesomelic dysplasia, a hereditary condition associated with severe growth reduction and limb shortening. Her remains had previously suggested acromesomelic dysplasia, but bones alone could not confirm it. Romito 1, believed to be her mother, had one altered copy of the gene and was shorter than average, consistent with carrier status. The finding shows that rare genetic disorders existed in human populations before modern medicine and can be identified through palaeogenomics. Ancient DNA gives researchers a way to investigate inherited conditions and trace genetic disorders in human lives before written records.What does Romito 2 reveal about care and support in prehistoric societyThe discovery also offers a glimpse into how prehistoric communities may have supported people with significant physical limitations. Romito 2 survived into late adolescence despite severe growth reduction and shortened limbs, which could have made movement difficult in a mobile hunter-gatherer society. Researchers suggest that her survival may point to sustained social care from members of her community. She may have relied on others for food and assistance while travelling. However, the evidence cannot show exactly how this support was provided, so researchers present it as an interpretation rather than a certainty.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Hit them hard’: Does Trump have another ‘new’ Iran strategy, can it work?
articles.summary: Trump signals harsher response as US-Iran hostilities escalate, raising fears of prolonged conflict in the Gulf region.
articles.body:
Following the first strikes in the US-Iran war for a month, this week, United States President Donald Trump appeared to signal a new phase in the war, which marked its first six months on Friday last week.

“We’re going to hit them hard … there will be a response,” Trump told reporters on Monday, shortly after Iran launched missile attacks on US military sites in Jordan in response to its strikes on Iran’s Larak Island the previous night.

US news outlet Axios reported Washington may be switching to a new “no war, no peace” strategy in the conflict in which it aims to hit Iran periodically without engaging in a sustained conflict.

So, what exactly is Trump’s strategy now, and can the US military sustain it as the war enters its seventh month?

The US struck military targets on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz, close to Iran’s strategic port of Bandar Abbas. Washington said its forces hit two Iranian rocket launchers which it claimed the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was preparing to use to scatter sea mines into the strait.

Iranian media reported three people were killed. Iran subsequently launched missiles at two airbases hosting US military personnel and assets in Jordan. Jordan said it intercepted eight missiles. In turn, Trump pledged to respond, saying: “ We’re going to hit them hard. ”

Speaking at a Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said his forces would cease fire if the US did the same, and if it fulfilled its commitments under ‌an interim deal signed in June to end the war, lift sanctions and open the Strait of Hormuz. That deal has since expired, however, and largely fell apart because of disagreements arising from its vague wording.

Monday’s exchange of fire marked the first direct attacks between the two sides in more than a month and raised fears that the conflict could return to a more intense military phase.

Trump, however, told media that the renewed fighting did not necessarily mean a return to full-scale war, saying the Strait of Hormuz is in “extremely good shape” while claiming Iran’s financial system, military, and leadership had been largely degraded.

“That doesn’t mean we won’t smack them. We’ll see what happens,” he told reporters at the White House.

How has the US war strategy shifted during the conflict?

The Trump administration’s approach to the war on Iran has been ever-changing. It began with a full-blown military campaign that lasted for 40 days, followed by a ceasefire which was later extended.

In June, Tehran and Washington signed a memorandum of understanding ( MoU ), agreeing to terms for a ceasefire and allowing wider peace talks for 60 days.

The woolly wording of the MoU, especially related to who had overall control of the Strait of Hormuz, caused it to collapse within weeks, with the US and Iran blaming each other for violating its terms. That led to a renewal of US attacks on Iran in July, with Tehran again retaliating against US military assets and other infrastructure in neighbouring Gulf countries.

More recently, the Trump administration shifted from sustained military action to economic pressure instead. That shift came amid US media reports that its forces were running low on munitions in the Middle East, particularly in supplies of critical Patriot interceptor missiles used to defend against Iranian drone and missile strikes. The Trump administration denies it is running out of weapons, however.

Last week, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced an economic pressure campaign against Iran, declaring that it would target its financial interests across the world.

He said the US would target Iran’s revenue sources, including oil; sanctioned 60 “entities” it claimed were facilitating Iranian oil sales; and threatened other countries and companies doing business with Tehran with the possibility of secondary sanctions .

On Monday, Bessent said the Iranian strikes were evidence Tehran was “lashing out kinetically because they are losing economically”, arguing that the new sanctions were beginning to hurt it.

Iran’s Central Bank Governor Abdolnaser Hemmati responded, saying the assertion that its economy was collapsing was “incorrect”.

“I say to the American president that we have enough foreign currency,” he told a news conference.

Is the US heading to a ‘no war, no peace’ strategy?

The current situation increasingly resembles an unstable middle ground with solutions rapidly disappearing, observers say.

While neither side appears to be seeking an immediate return to full-scale war, both have demonstrated that they are prepared to respond militarily when they believe their interests are threatened.

On Monday, Axios reported the Trump administration is considering the strategy of periodically attacking Iran to keep moving oil tankers out of the Gulf region safely. The plan for a sporadic return to military strikes on Iran has yet to be approved by Trump, it reported.

Iran effectively closed the critical Strait of Hormuz in early March, following the start of the war and has not allowed it to operate fully since, letting only a few ships it deems “friendly” to pass at times. Now, both sides say they control the waterway, with Iran firing rockets intermittently at vessels attempting to get through without its approval, and Trump claiming the US Navy is successfully escorting ships.

Since the MoU broke down, with the US resuming strikes on Iran in July, Iran says it refuses to engage diplomatically with Washington, and has held talks only with Oman over the future administration of Hormuz.

Trita Parsi, director and cofounder of the US-based Quincy Institute, said, “To periodically bomb a country is to fight a forever war … there is no way around it.”

“The [Trump] administration seems to be giving up on solving the issue militarily, economically, or diplomatically, and instead resorting to permanent warfare to manage the problem,” he told Al Jazeera.

“An utter defeat from the US’s starting point of thinking the war would take no more than four days.”

Is Trump’s new strategy of sporadic warfare sustainable?

Analysts say there are a number of reasons the US may not be able to keep up the pressure on Iran indefinitely.

Mohammad Eslami, a research fellow at the University of Tehran, said the Trump administration is ultimately trying to pursue a “calculated” conflict with Iran for control of the strait, which had been entirely and freely open to all shipping before the war began.

“We should consider that this war was based on miscalculations in Washington, DC, and right now, it seems that they are very confident about their decisions” regarding the trajectory of the war on Iran, Eslami told Al Jazeera.

But the risk is that sporadic strikes, such as those which took place this week, will further escalate tensions in the region, he said.

Negar Mortazavi, senior fellow at the Washington, DC-based Center for International Policy, says renewed escalation became inevitable after the collapse of the MoU .

“Iran has made its position clear: if Washington returns to the MoU, Tehran will return as well; if the US continues to prioritise military pressure, Iran will escalate,” Mortazavi told Al Jazeera. “A mutual return to the MoU remains the clearest path to de-escalation.”

Otherwise, she warned, both sides risk losing control of the situation.

While Iran says it has reached a framework of agreement for the future management of the Strait of Hormuz with Oman, “the Americans are thinking that they don’t need any kind of diplomatic settlement right now”, Eslami added.

“[Instead] they want to wait until after the [US] November midterm elections” and continue exerting economic pressure on Iran, he said.

However, traffic through the strait remains at all-time lows, having slumped from about 100 ships a day to a daily average of seven through the war. Furthermore, Mortazavi said, “Tehran will not capitulate under [economic] pressure. Both sides may believe they can control the escalation, but every new exchange increases the risk of a wider regional conflict.”

It is also unclear how long the US can keep up strikes on Iran – no matter how infrequent – due to speculation it is running low on munitions.

Then there is the political cost to Trump of sustaining the war. His approval rating at home has fallen to 33 percent as higher petrol prices and the prolonged war have created growing domestic pressure for him.

The war on Iran began as a joint US-Israeli military campaign, but the two countries now appear to have differing priorities.

Last month, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reiterated that he was determined to prevent Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons, despite a lack of evidence Tehran is currently pursuing one.

Israel has officially struck Iran only once since April’s initial ceasefire took effect, but it has been obstructive regarding the June MoU, refusing to withdraw from southern Lebanon despite the agreement stipulating a ceasefire on all fronts.

However, the US’s priority is finding an exit from the war, which includes reopening the Strait of Hormuz and reducing the economic and political costs of the conflict, as it heads towards midterm elections in November.

Parsi of Quincy Institute said the two allies’ interests no longer converge. “The US does not have an interest in eternal war with Iran.”

articles.title: Woman hospitalized with possible shark bite on Martha’s Vineyard
articles.summary: A swimmer suffered a leg injury believed to be from a shark bite Monday afternoon, according to officials on Martha’s Vineyard.
articles.body: A swimmer suffered a leg injury believed to be from a shark bite Monday afternoon, according to officials on Martha’s Vineyard. James Hagerty, town administrator in Edgartown, Massachusetts, said emergency crews responded around 1:40 p.m. to Norton Point after a woman in her late 20s was injured. The wounds to the woman’s leg are consistent with a marine animal’s bite, but no shark or other animal was observed, Hagerty said. He added that the woman’s injuries are non-life-threatening and do not involve the loss of a leg. The incident left South Beach closed to swimmers for several hours as the town assesses safety conditions. “The Town appreciates the prompt response of emergency personnel and beach staff,” Hagerty wrote. “Beachgoers are reminded to remain aware of their surroundings while in the water and to comply with instructions from lifeguards and any posted beach advisories.”
